en: *The Treatise on Opening the Mind and Revealing the Nature in the Mahāyāna:
An Immediate Awakening to the True Principle*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Dazhao and the Layman Huiguang.
Now, the Great Way integrates the mind and reveals the reality of the single principle. The sages and worthies of past and present have all sought only this gateway.
The awakened realize that the three realms are mind-only.
Those who do not awaken follow the latent tendencies. In the school of the *Yānāvatāra*, the principle is definitively established through the manifestation of characteristics.
One who has true realization knows that all phenomena are quiescent; things are established through causes and conditions, and names are formed through provisional synthesis.
Those who do not understand this are attached to names and dwell upon words; they grasp at signs and are driven by delusion.
If one wishes to gather the false back into the true and realize the equality of defilement and purity, one must vigilantly observe the mind.
Fundamental enlightenment manifests of itself;
although mental contemplation possesses power,
it still does not transcend the realm of thought and intention to reach the other shore.
He constantly entered profound meditative concentration;
having practiced this for a long time without ceasing,
all matters were naturally brought to completion.
If one contemplates that phenomena within the locus gradually incline toward the truth,
then even if the body and mind are relaxed and expansive, their dissolution remains clear;
though activity arises, it is eternally quiescent— an illumination that does not conform to forms.
Spontaneous samādhi nurtures virtue through its path; it provides the sustenance for the completion of the Dharma-body,
such that one returns to awakening at the source of the mind without hindrance or obstruction.
When the essence is like empty space, it is called the Samādhi of Boundlessness.
When the mind has no entering or exiting, it is called the Samādhi of Non-Quiescence.
When there is purity and no seeking amidst all places of existence, it is called the Samādhi of the Inconceivable.
This samādhi is neither obscured nor does it arise from conditions; it is called the Dharma-nature Samādhi.
All learners merely seek its understanding and do not seek personal realization.
If one wishes to practice the Mahāyāna, [one must realize this].
Not understanding how to settle the mind, he knew for certain that his realization had been lost. At that time,
there was a layman of secular surname Li named Huiguang.
He was a native of Chang’an in Yongzhou.
His Dharma name was Dazhao.
He disregarded honor and profit.
He resolved to seek Bodhi;
he served Master An as his preceptor and later served Master Hui as his abbot.
They have all personally received the oral instructions and been granted the secret transmission of the essential teachings.
As for their mastery of the refined meanings and subtle principles— reaching the root and exhausting the source—
they transcend existence and enter non-existence, attaining perfect, harmonious, and sovereign freedom.
During his leisure from meditative contemplation, the lay practitioner sighed over these deluded masses;
he then revealed the profound gateway of phenomena and principle,
presented the subtle meanings, and opened up these essential teachings of the Dharma.
It may be said that this vessel for crossing the ocean proceeds directly toward Bodhi;
these words are indeed true.
It is my hope that those who have not yet attained awakening may thereby be led to awakening.
"May those who are not yet at peace attain peace;
may those who are not yet liberated attain liberation.
The householder then asked:
The Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle; ordinary people do not perceive it.
The texts are vast and extensive, making their meaning difficult to understand.
I ask the Chan Master for the essentials of the Dharma, setting aside for a moment expedient means.
Speaking directly and truthfully, he does not discard the common flow.
Fortunately, there is no secret [to be hidden]. Master Dazhao replied:
"Excellent, excellent! Observe what you have asked."
The Bodhisattva’s roots of capacity appear to be nearly matured.
My stature is forty-five *zhang*,
and it has been more than twenty years since I entered the Way.
Never before has anyone asked about this meaning.
What matter do you have, and what doubt do you wish to resolve?
Ask directly and speak plainly; there is no need for prolixity. He asked:

Now, for one who wishes to enter the Way, what dharmas should they cultivate? What dharmas should they observe? What dharmas should they realize? What dharmas should they seek? What dharmas should they awaken to? And by obtaining what dharmas do they proceed toward Bodhi? The answer is:
When not observing even a single dharma, there is nothing to seek;
when not realizing even a single dharma, there is no subsequent state;
when not awakening to even a single dharma, there is no path to be cultivated.
"This is itself bodhi. [The disciple] asked:
"Since beginningless time, I, your disciple, have wandered through birth and death, acting in opposition to the principle."
Upon first hearing the doctrine of sudden enlightenment, one is bewildered and knows nothing;
the spirit and consciousness grow dim, and one is unaware of where they are.
It is like a drunken man who cannot yet attain clear awakening.
I humbly pray that you will reach down to those who are deluded and grant us a few moments of your inquiry, so that through skillful means we may realize the truth. Question:
What is the true nature? Answer: [The true nature is]... (text continues)
The mind does not arise; it is eternally signless and pure. Question:
What is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? Answer:
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as all phenomena (*dharma*), each have their own intrinsic nature, which is perceived through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Question:
"From what does intrinsic nature arise? He replied, "It arises from the deluded mind.
Again he asked, "How is one free from intrinsic nature? He replied:
When the mind does not arise, one is detached. Question: What is the path?
What is the principle?
"What is this mind? He replied, "The mind is the Path;
the mind is the Principle."
Thus, there is no principle apart from the mind,
and no mind apart from principle.
That the mind is able to be impartial is what is called "principle."
The illumination of principle that can clarify is called the mind;
the equality of principle and mind is called the Buddha-mind.
One who attains this principle does not perceive birth and death.
Ordinary beings and sages are no different;
object and wisdom are non-dual;
principle and phenomena are both harmoniously integrated.
Defilement and purity are of one suchness;
when there is true illumination according to reality,
there is nothing that is not the Way.
Self and other are both transcended;
all practices are performed simultaneously,
without before or after, and without middle.
Mastery over bondage and liberation is what is called the Way. Question:
Who is a person who accords with correct principle? Answer: [A person who]...
The mind does not arise; it is constantly in accord with signlessness. Question:
How is one in accord with the Path? Answer:
A straightforward mind that does not cling to anything is itself in accord. Question: [How so?]
Question: What is delusion? Answer:
Not recognizing one's own mind is delusion. Question: What is inversion? Answer:
If various objective realms arise, this is perversion. Question:
What is the self-mind? What is the deluded mind? Answer:
If one engages in discrimination, it is the deluded mind;
non-discrimination is one's own true mind. Question:
From what do the discriminating mind and the non-discriminating mind arise? Answer:
Discriminating mind arises from inversion;
non-discriminating mind arises from right knowledge. Question:
From what do both discriminating mind and non-discriminating mind arise? Answer:
Regarding the "absence of a place of birth": Question:
Since there is no place of birth, why is it said that there are inversions (*viparyāsa*) and why is it said that there is correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)? Answer:
If one does not recognize one’s own mind, one engages in various inversions; if one recognizes one’s own mind, that itself is correct knowledge. Question: [What is this?]
"Now, from what do both recognition and non-recognition arise? Answer:
"If recognition arises from awakening, then non-recognition arises from deluded conceptualization. Question: "..."
"All sentient beings are entirely within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Are they also within right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?
He replied, "All sentient beings do not abide in right knowledge."
"In reality, there is no deluded thought. Question:
"In my present state, how can these deluded appearances be called 'right knowledge'? Answer:
"From the very beginning, you have truly had no deluded thoughts."
What is now called "false conceptualization" is like a person who, having eaten hemp seeds, searches for a needle in the air;
yet in such empty space, there is truly no needle. Question:
Question: Since there has never been delusion from the very beginning, what is it that all practitioners of the Way must now sever in order to seek the Way? Answer:
One does not sever a single thing, nor is there any Way to be sought. Question: Why is this so?
Since there is no path to be sought and no object to be severed,
why does the World-Honored One state in the sūtras that one must sever deluded thoughts? The answer is as follows:
World-Honored One, you truly do not teach the severing of deluded thoughts.

If one were to sever deluded thoughts, that would mean not being free from the deluded attainment and deluded severance of all sentient beings, as well as the false views regarding the existence of deluded phenomena.
The World-Honored One speaks of falsely established, illusory dharmas in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings;
yet in reality, the World-Honored One does not speak even a single word of illusory dharmas.
It is like a skilled physician prescribing medicine according to the specific ailment.
If there were no illness, one would not speak of medicine. Question:
Since the World-Honored One has stated that all phenomena are illusory conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), who is it that creates these conceptualizations? Answer:
Sentient beings create [their own states] for themselves;
thus, right wisdom is non-existent. Question:
Why is it that right wisdom does not create?
[The interlocutor] asks: "Is it because of the biased fabrication of deluded thoughts? [The Master] replies:
"If one does not recognize right wisdom, there are deluded thoughts.
If one recognizes deluded thoughts... [The interlocutor] asks:
If right knowledge already exists, then conceptualization should likewise exist;
why, then, do you say that there is no conceptualization? He replied:
Sentient beings truly have neither false conceptualization nor correct wisdom;
both are unobtainable. Question:
Since both are unattainable, it follows that there would be neither ordinary person nor sage. [The opponent] replies:
There are indeed ordinary persons and there are indeed sages.
"You yourself do not recognize it. He asked:
"Which is the ordinary person, and which is the noble one? He replied:
"If you engage in conceptual discrimination, you are an ordinary person."
If non-discrimination is itself the noble one, [the interlocutor] asks:
"Discrimination is ordinary;
non-discrimination is the noble."
"If one does not discriminate like a small infant with a long head,
can such a person be considered a sage? He replied,
"To hold such a view is to be a great fool."
It is like an infant who, being young and immature, does not distinguish between good and evil;
it is like a fool who does not recognize the distinction between the noble and the base.
How could this not be a non-discriminating realization?
One must constantly practice discernment within the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) so that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) may arise. Question:
Is the mere non-arising of mental activity not itself non-conceptual wisdom? Answer: No.
For now, observe the place of observation, observe the pure mind, and observe the place where the mind arises.
You must then awaken to the fact that the mind has been pure from the very beginning and is not defiled by external conditions.
One must see that phenomena are thoroughly understood;
since the nature of causes and conditions cannot be apprehended,
one knows that causes and conditions are both empty and not empty.
This refers to all the myriad phenomena of the world—rulers and subjects, parents and children, human righteousness, propriety, and trustworthiness.
These are the worldly dharmas that are indestructible.
Therefore, the scriptural text states that one enters nirvana without destroying worldly dharmas.
If one destroys the worldly dharmas, one is a common person wandering through birth and death.
These worldly causal conditions have no individual master;
they are merely a combination of conditions, their essential nature being entirely empty.
Ultimately, the object cannot be apprehended.
If one perceives this principle, it is called seeing the nature;
this is precisely what it means.
Within conceptualization itself, one attains non-conceptual wisdom;
though constantly engaged in conceptualization, one does not conceptualize.
This is the non-destruction of worldly dharmas.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"To discern the characteristics of the various fetters while entering the primary meaning (paramārtha) without wavering.
Thus, one who is able to awaken is precisely that which moves and yet gives rise to stillness. Again, it was asked:
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"Constantly seek the wisdom of non-conceptual true contemplation;
regarding worldly dharmas, have few desires and be content."
One seeks the supramundane dharmas without weariness;
while not violating one’s majestic deportment, one is able to manifest supernatural powers in accordance with worldly customs to lead sentient beings toward the Path.
What is the meaning of this? The answer is:
This meaning is precisely the wondrousness of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
That which realizes it is wisdom, not that which is fathomed by the mind. A question is asked:
"Since one constantly seeks non-thought and true contemplation," [how is this so?]
On account of what matter do the various sūtras speak of the merit of giving and observing precepts as that of humans and devas?
Is this not indeed mindfulness of the Dharma?
For what reason do they differ and possess distinctions, causing all students of the Way to harbor doubts and lack faith? He replied:
"Do not disbelieve."
You do not understand the matter.
When the Buddha spoke of the blessings of giving and observing the precepts as leading to the realms of devas and humans,
it was because sentient beings mostly dwell in conceptual construction.
The Buddha possesses immeasurable skillful means;
according to the inclinations of sentient beings, he teaches them that phenomena are illusory,
thereby inducing them to enter the gateway of the Mahāyāna.
Since you do not believe this now,
I shall cite a scripture to provide proof.
The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
These ninefold teachings of mine are expounded in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, yet the Mahāyāna is their fundamental basis.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle."
Furthermore, one uses provisional names to lead sentient beings toward the Way;
one never uses the Lesser Vehicle to ferry sentient beings across.
It is also said:
Do not associate with those who study the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, it is said:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real."
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"If a person discriminates regarding the precepts,
there is no precept at all."
If one perceives that there is a precept,
this is itself the loss of the precept;
it is according to this principle.
One should know that when the Buddha speaks of the gate of ultimate reality, he does not say that people lack merit;
rather, he merely guides sentient beings to enter the wisdom of the Buddha.
When the sages of the past and present speak of attaining mastery of the mind, liberation of the mind, and becoming a sage through the mind, they mean this.
"This is the Great Seal of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, which shatters your doubts. Question:
"If the Buddhas teach the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) for the sake of transforming and guiding all sentient beings,"
"If you have now attained total awakening, why must you continue to speak of deluding sentient beings?
Would this not incur transgression? He replied:
Do not give rise to such a thought.
Because the Buddhas possess great compassion,
those among sentient beings who fall into the three evil realms are numerous.
Therefore, for those who hear the gateway of skillful means, the six pāramitās are taught.
As for the pāramitās: they are giving, ethical discipline, patience, and exertion.
By practicing these three things, one attains liberation from the three evil paths and comes and goes among humans and devas.
By practicing diligence, meditative concentration,
and wisdom— these three things— one attains liberation from the suffering of birth and death.
Regarding the future attainment of Buddhahood:
it is asked, "Did the Buddhas of the past teach the three vehicles?
Or did the Buddhas of the present teach the three vehicles? It is answered: [They did].
The Buddhas of the past, present, and future are collectively described [as such]. Question:
By what principle or reasoning is this known? Answer:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
If one were to praise only the Buddha-vehicle,
sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma.
Because they would reject the Dharma and lack faith,
they would fall into the three evil realms; therefore,
I would rather not preach the Dharma.
He quickly entered nirvana,
reflecting upon the power of the skillful means practiced by past Buddhas:
"The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles."
Knowing that the Buddhas of the past all taught the three vehicles to guide sentient beings and lead them into the one vehicle—Question:
What is this one vehicle? Answer:
The mind is the One Vehicle. Question:
How is it known that the mind is the One Vehicle? Answer:
It can be seen that the mind is empty and possesses nothing.
"This is precisely the One Vehicle. Question:
"If realizing that the mind is empty and non-existent is the One Vehicle, does one thereby attain sainthood? Answer:
"One attains sainthood. Question again: "..."
"Is there an ordinary person? He replied, "There is also an ordinary person. Question:
"Is there a difference between the ordinary person and the noble one, or not? Answer: "..."
There is no difference at all.
If one awakens, one is a commoner in the morning and a sage by evening;
if one does not awaken, one undergoes rebirth within the six realms. Question: [What is the cause of this?]
Question: What is it that awakens at the time of awakening? Answer: It is the mind that awakens. Question:
Are the ordinary mind and the sage’s mind one or two? Answer: [They are one.]
"This is one. What is this "one"? The answer is:
To clearly perceive that the nature of phenomena is pure, being without defilement or attachment from the very beginning—this is to know it as "one. Question:
Who knows that which is unstained and unattached? The answer is:
the mind knows that which is unstained. The question is:
how does the mind know that which is unstained? The answer is:
The Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught that the mind has no form or substance and is ultimately unattainable.
By this, one knows it is unstained. Question: Since it has no form or substance, how can it be unstained?
How is it known that there is no defilement? The answer is:
Precisely because it has no physical form, one knows there is no defilement.
If there are signs, locations, or even defilements present—Question:
As previously stated, you spoke of the "mind.
I do not yet know how many types of mind there are in total. Answer:
If you awaken to it, the one mind is unattainable;
if you do not awaken to it, there are various kinds of minds whose number cannot be known. Question:
Is this the mind of an ordinary person?
"What is the noble mind? He replied:
"If you grasp at signs, that is the mundane mind;
to be free from signs is the noble mind. He asked:
"Please show me the essential point regarding the mind that grasps at signs and the mind that does not grasp at signs. He replied:
"For all those who cultivate the path, if they perceive the coming and going of the mind, this is precisely the long-extending mind."
Seeing good and evil;
seeing hatred and love;
seeing anger and joy.
Seeing the heterodox and the orthodox;
seeing the ordinary and the sage;
seeing the autonomous and the non-autonomous.
One sees nirvana;
one sees liberation;
one sees non-liberation.
One sees Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
one sees the ultimate and the non-ultimate;
one sees those with understanding and knowledge and those without understanding and knowledge.
"Seeing diligence,
seeing meditative concentration,
and seeing wisdom," and so forth.
These are all the deluded minds of ordinary people. Question:
What is the mind of a sage? Answer:
Not giving rise to a single thought, nor perceiving a single thing.
"This is precisely the mind of the sages. Question:
"Does the Chan Master possess the mind of the sages? Answer:
"I, too, have no attainment. Question: "..."
Since there is nothing attained, how can there be knowing? He replied:
"I now neither attain nor know.
Therefore, a sutra says:"
There is neither ignorance nor attainment.
That which is non-attainment is itself a bodhisattva. Question:
To whom does this principle ultimately belong? Answer: [It belongs to no one.]
Not a single thing belongs to anything.
If there were anything to which one belonged,
that would be the cycle of birth and death.
If it has no point of attachment, it is ultimately and eternally abiding. Question:
All sentient beings revolve through the eight consciousnesses and do not attain mastery.
What are these eight consciousnesses? The answer is:
they are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, manas, and ālaya.
As for what is called "consciousness":
It has discernment as its essential meaning;
for example, when the eye is in conjunction with visible forms, the mental consciousness discriminates therein,
sometimes reckoning them as beautiful.
Alternatively, when one calculates what is evil,
as soon as that calculation gives rise to a mental image, it immediately perfumes the seventh manas-consciousness;
because of this perfuming, one subsequently grasps at it.
It perfumes the eighth consciousness in turn;
because it stores all accumulated seeds of karma, it is named the "storehouse" (ālaya). As it is with the visual consciousness, so it is with the others.
The various consciousnesses are likewise.
For all sentient beings who experience the retribution of their karma,
they first take the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and, through successive transformation, act as the cause for the three types of karma of the future.
Because they rely on causes and perceive them as causes, and ride upon fruits and perceive them as fruits without interruption,
they ultimately return to the six realms to undergo the suffering of birth and death.
Therefore, those who have not yet realized the mind are deluded by the eight consciousnesses.
Regarding what is called these eight consciousnesses:
they are said to have the fundamental nature as their cause,
arising in dependence upon present conditions.
The formation of causes and conditions comes together;
yet one still desires to produce the causes for the future.
Now, one wishes to sever these so that they do not arise.
When practicing correct contemplation, one should discern from where visual consciousness arises:
does it arise from form,
or does it arise from the eye?
Is it obtained from the mind?
If it were obtained from the mind, then even a blind person would possess it, for they too have a mind.
How is it that [the visual faculty] cannot produce eye-consciousness?
If a dead person possesses eyes...
How is it that one cannot discern form?
If [consciousness] were derived from form,
then form would be insentient, obstructive, and devoid of cognition.
When one realizes that these various conditions cannot independently discern the mind, one then knows that at the time of seeing a form with the eye,
the causal condition of the eye is empty. Since the causal condition of the eye is empty...
This is precisely the emptiness of form.
If one realizes that the essence of these three things is empty, there is no conceptual differentiation.
Because there is no conceptual differentiation, the consciousness differentiates while remaining without differentiation.
The seven consciousnesses desire to grasp, yet there is nothing to grasp;
within the eighth consciousness, the storehouse, there is no further perfuming;
because the seeds of defilement are absent, there are no seeds.
Furthermore, one no longer craves birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
One abides in profound stillness and permanence, neither being produced by birth nor extinguished by death. Question: [Why is this so?]
Question: From what are the three bodies of the Buddha obtained? Answer:
The three bodies of the Buddha are obtained from the eight consciousnesses;
by transforming the eight consciousnesses, the four wisdoms are realized.
These four wisdoms are condensed into the three bodies (trikāya).
This constitutes the distinction of the three bodies from cause to fruition. Question:
By what reasoning is this known? The answer is:

because these five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—are taken as the wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna).
The sixth consciousness is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done;
the seventh manas-consciousness is the Wisdom of Equality;
and the seventh ālaya-vijñāna is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Question:
For what purpose is this statement made regarding these four knowledges? The answer is:
the five preceding consciousnesses are also called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
These five faculties are the gates of wisdom that illuminate and contact external objects without delusive defilement.
Therefore, these five consciousnesses are taken as the wisdom of wondrous observation.
As for the sixth consciousness, it is also called the mental faculty (*manas*);
this gateway of wisdom must be diligently awakened to.
Awakening is immediately pure;
it accords with the Dharma,
and by observing both the ultimate and conventional truths simultaneously, one accomplishes wisdom.
The transformation of the mind results in wisdom;
wisdom illuminates with clarity,
while consciousness is devoid of discrimination.
The transformation of wisdom is called the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). As for the seventh *manas* consciousness, it no longer grasps;
naturally, it is without aversion and without attachment.
Because it is free from hatred and attachment, all phenomena are entirely equal;
therefore, it is called the Wisdom of Equality.
Within the eighth ālayavijñāna-store, it is emptiness itself.
The seeds of all afflictions are entirely purified,
like a clear mirror suspended in space,
wherein all myriad phenomena appear.
Yet this bright mirror never gives rise to the thought,
"I am able to manifest images," nor does the image say anything at all.
"I arise from the mirror;
there is neither agent nor object.
Therefore, this wisdom is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Question:
Since the four wisdoms are thus, what are the three bodies? The answer is:
the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom constitutes the Dharmakāya.
The wisdom of equality constitutes the reward body (saṃbhogakāya);
the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done and the wisdom of wondrous observation constitute the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). Again, it was asked:
"By what means is this known such that you make this statement? He replied:
In terms of the present time,
it is endowed with all the qualities of meditative concentration and the perfection of all untainted virtues;
it is like a bright mirror in the world that manifests the images of various faces without discrimination.
Therefore, this knowledge is said to be the Dharma-body.
Once deluded mind is exhausted,
the nature of equality is realized and the myriad practices are perfected.
This is considered the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya),
which, with its six sense faculties free from defilement, extensively delivers sentient beings,
liberating both oneself and others.
To cause others to likewise understand and cultivate the causes [of enlightenment], he therefore employs transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Question:
How does one cause all sentient beings to desire to seek Buddhahood?
Among the three bodies, which body should be cultivated first? The answer is:
A sūtra states that the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) flows forth from the equal dharma body (dharmakāya).
From this Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) flows forth the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya);
from this Transformation Body flow forth the teachings of the Three Piṭakas and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
For this reason, one first cultivates the Dharmakāya.
What is called the Dharma-body is the Middle Way of correct contemplation regarding wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence.
If one awakens to this principle, that is the Dharma-body.
By perceiving the Dharma-body, one knows that one's own body and mind have, from time immemorial, constantly been in opposition to it.
Having seen the Dharma, one must immediately apply oneself with diligence.
By applying the mind diligently and without interruption, one naturally becomes pure.
Because this accords with suchness (*tathatā*), it remains so for as long as it does not cease.
When the mind has thus been perfected,
this constitutes the Reward Buddha (saṃbhogakāya).
Therefore, while the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is inherently present, the Reward-body is realized through cultivation.
Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), a sutra states:
"Manifesting various bodies is called the transformation body. A question is asked:
Since the three bodies of the Buddha are thus, what are the Three Jewels? The answer is:
the three bodies of the Buddha are also called the Three Jewels.
Regarding what are called the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel: Question:
How many kinds of Three Jewels are there? Answer:
If explained in full detail:
There are three kinds of Triple Gem. Question:
What are these three called? Answer:
The single-essence Triple Gem.
The Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics and the Three Jewels of Sustaining Maintenance. Question:
What are the Three Jewels of One Essence? Answer:
The essence of the true mind is the purity of the nature of awakening;
this is called the perfection of the Buddha Jewel. That it possesses functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is called the Dharma Jewel.
The meaning of the functional aspect is that of a single essence and a single flavor;
this is called the Sangha Jewel. Question:
What are the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels? Answer:
As for the distinct characteristic, this very self is called the Buddha Jewel;
it is also able to administer medicine according to the capacities of others and desires to practice for itself.
These are called the Jewel of the Dharma.
The harmony of the four great elements and the five aggregates, being without mutual conflict, are all called the Jewel of the Sangha. Question:
What is meant by "upholding the Three Jewels"? The answer is:
"Upholding" refers to being truly capable of supporting those above and assisting those below, ensuring that all matters are pure and harmonious.
That which is named the Jewel of the Buddha is that which,
when spoken according to one's inclination, brings joy to those who hear it;
this is named the Jewel of the Dharma.
Being among the assembly, they do not contravene the ten thousand practices; through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they can harmonize all things and engage in no contentious debate.
This is called the Jewel of the Sangha. Question: Why is it designated as a "jewel"? Answer:
This ultimate truth does not exist internally, externally, or in between;
it cannot be measured, nor has it a value or price.
To illustrate this by way of analogy:
It is called the Three Jewels.
If something has a price, it is not called a jewel;
therefore, it is said that the wish-fulfilling priceless jewel is [the analogy]. Question:
The *Laojing* says:
"The Way of the Buddha acts, yet there is nothing it does not do.
What is the meaning of this? The answer is:
The Buddha-way is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Sentient beings give rise to the view of self as vast as Mount Sumeru,
and thus it becomes conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This meaning is not something known by the intellect (*manas*) nor fathomed by the mind (*citta*);
it is realized through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). One can only achieve proficiency through such practice.
At one time there was a great awakening. A question was asked:
"The Sūtra says that all dharmas emerge from this sūtra. The answer was given:
"The 'sūtra' is the mind."
The mind can manifest all things;
when the practitioner cultivates the unimpeded, perfect illumination,
the cause for the supreme right path is thereby revealed.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, first cultivate themselves and finally transform sentient beings;
there is no dharma that they do not encompass.
Therefore it is said: "All [dharmas] emerge from this sutra. Question:
The Sūtra says: "To shoulder the burden for the Tathāgata—what is the meaning of this? Answer:
You need only reflect back upon your own nature, without dwelling in permanence.
In retrospect, he realized there is no self;
who, then, could bear the burden?
Having deeply penetrated Prajñāpāramitā, he extensively expounded it for others.
This is precisely to shoulder the burden of the True Dharma and transport the ultimate meaning, causing all sentient beings to accomplish merit and virtue;
therefore, it is said that one "shoulders the burden for the Tathāgata. Question:
The Sūtra says:
"The Tathāgata delivers sentient beings.
What is the meaning of this? Answer:
You yourself have realized that the true nature of sentient beings is fundamentally pure; yet,
when the characteristics of the six sense organs arise,
the disease of afflictions is produced.
When one contemplates that birth is fundamentally empty, what is there to be delivered? Therefore,
if one says that the Tathāgata delivers [beings], [it is not so].
[They] immediately cling to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a recipient. [The interlocutor] asks:
"Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, what is its meaning? [The respondent] answers:
Vajra refers to form and mind;
Prajñā refers to purity;
Pāra refers to the other shore.
"Mi" means arrival. He asked again:
"If one does not grasp at appearances, remaining as such without moving, [what then? He replied:
"If your mind arises, there is going and coming."
Thus, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are of the nature of instability.
When your mind does not arise, there is neither coming nor going; this is the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Within the unconditioned, one is detached from both movement and stillness.
This is precisely what is eternally abiding;
therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā), which is immovable. Question:
The *Jiaosheshi wenshi jing* (Sutra on the Warm Bathhouse) says:
By providing these seven items and bathing the assembly of monks, one obtains immeasurable merit.
Regarding the meaning and significance of this merit, please provide an explanation. He replied:
As the Sūtra says:
What has been said is indeed true and not false.
If you bathe while possessing these seven items,
there must be a correspondence between your inner state and outer conduct, whereby your merit and blessings will be immeasurable.
You who have first bathed using these seven items— charcoal, fire, warm pure water, clear ash, beans, a willow branch, and oil for the inner garments—
yet whose nature you constantly toy with and allow greed and anger to run wild.
To scold, strike, or engage in disputes with others until they shed tears and blood is itself the shedding of the Buddha’s own blood;
it is the constant cultivation of karma leading to the three miserable realms.
One who bathes in this manner is like one washing a moat;
when the mud is exhausted, one should desist.
It is simply that body and mind are purified, and greed and anger do not arise.
Natural equality is itself free from conceptual discrimination.
Having already distinguished between water and washing, all dust and grime are removed, or rather, it is fundamentally pure. It is asked:
If one wishes to counteract these three poisons of the mind and accomplish the six pāramitās, the answer is:
You must apply courageous and diligent effort to the mind, and in opposition to the three poisons, you must give rise to the three vows.
I vow to sever all evil.
Regarding the poison of anger,
I vow to cultivate all that is wholesome.
Regarding the poison of delusion,
I vow for all sentient beings;
regarding the poison of craving.
By means of being able to sever and cultivate attachments,
one brings together the three poisons within the mind and accomplishes the formation of the three clusters of pure precepts.
Next, to clarify those of inferior resolve:
one who develops five kinds of inferior resolve toward the five aggregates is as follows.
First, they vow to regard all sentient beings as noble sages while regarding themselves as ordinary worldlings.
Second, one vows to regard all sentient beings as kings and oneself as a commoner.
Third, one vows to regard all sentient beings as teachers and monks and oneself as a disciple.
Fourth, one vows to regard all sentient beings as one's own parents and to conceive of oneself as their son or daughter.
Fifth, one vows to regard all sentient beings as one's masters and to conceive of oneself as their servant or slave.
The six pāramitās are also called the six perfections:
giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
These six correspond respectively to the purification of the six sense faculties.
Not arising within the six realms and being without attachment to either internal or external things, one naturally practices giving;
this encompasses the dāna-pāramitā.
Good and evil are equal, as both are ultimately unattainable.
This encompasses the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).
When object and wisdom are brought into harmony and all conflict and harm are forever exhausted,
this encompasses the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
In great quiescence and immobility, the myriad practices are spontaneous;
this encompasses the perfection of diligence.
Amidst the profuse arising of phenomena, the wondrous stillness of the Dharmakāya manifests of itself.
It encompasses the dhyāna-pāramitā;
it is wondrously quiescent, luminous, immutable, ultimately eternal, and unattached to anything.
It encompasses the prajñā-pāramitā.
These are called the six pāramitās.
In the language of India, they are called pāramitās;
in the language of Han, they mean "reaching the other shore. Question:
"Ordinary people have traditionally found that questions and answers give rise to mental afflictions and confusion.
Master, you bestow [this teaching] with such joy that I have no small doubt;
I have not yet dared to follow my own inclinations."
Fearing it might cause you fatigue and vexation, the Zen Master replied:
"If you have no doubts, there is no need for forced questioning.
The Dharma has no answers to be given."
There would then be high and low among dharmas;
that which is without question and without answer is the equality of dharmas.
If one were to extensively seek views and understandings, [one would fall into error].
One immediately loses the original path,
and it also acts as an obstacle to knowledge within your mind,
causing your mind to give rise to [the view of] annihilation.
If you truly have doubts or obstructions, you must inquire with diligence;
all these are for the purpose of realizing the truth. Someone asked:
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"One is far removed from the perceiver and the perceived.
What is the meaning of this? The answer is:
When thoughts cease to arise, the mind becomes peaceful and secure. A question was asked:
"Although I am a layperson, my consciousness has long since entered the Way."
Wen said: "I have now heard the Master’s teaching that all these are the correct, true, and unsurpassed Bodhi.
My vow is fulfilled and my mind shall never regress.
I shall suddenly sever all worldly ties, so that the mind and the six consciousnesses are unified in the state of non-abiding."
With single-minded devotion, they yearned and looked up with longing;
their voices and tears fell together,
unable to be restrained.
Upon understanding this, I was momentarily overcome with shame and wept bitterly;
within my five viscera, I contemplated with heart-rending pain,
lamenting that for many kalpas I have been deluded regarding this True Principle.
Had it not been for the compassionate pity of Master Buniyin,
the common people would have had no way to attain awakening;
thus it is said:
The Great Treatise on Liberation.
If the author of this treatise accords with the intention of the Sage, [then it is authoritative].
May all sentient beings share equally in this merit.
If it does not accord with the holy intention, may my transgressions be extinguished.
Should there be any non-human beings [who seek to obstruct], may they not be able to transmit [this teaching].
I fear that [this person] might incidentally destroy the wisdom of the Dharma.
If there is a person of true realization whose merit is profound,
they should transmit the Dharma of the Great Way to those who cherish it.
It must not be shown lightly;
one must not take pleasure in contentious debate,
but should instead maintain a silent mind.
Knowing for oneself that deluded thoughts do not arise and that the mind of "mine" is extinguished:
this is the Mahāyāna Treatise on Opening the Mind to Reveal Liberation.
